title: Failure detection and membership
subtitle: A cluster must decide when a node is dead, but it can never be sure. Learn how heartbeats, phi accrual and SWIM gossip make that guess, and what goes wrong after it.

c.v: In September 2012, GitHub ran its main MySQL database on a 3-node cluster. A tool called Percona Replication Manager, running on Pacemaker, ran
health checks
on the primary. If the checks failed, it moved the "active" role to another server.
On Monday, a database migration put more load on the primary than the team had seen before. The primary was busy, not broken. But the load made its health checks fail.
So the cluster did what it was told. It moved the active role and the primary database to another server.
The new server had a cold
cache
, so it "performed rather poorly". Under real traffic, its health checks failed too. The active role moved back to the first server.
A GitHub engineer turned on Pacemaker's maintenance mode, which turns off all health checks and automatic
failover
. The site recovered slowly as the cache filled. After the incident, GitHub changed its setup so that only a person from operations starts a failover of the primary database.
The health check could not tell "busy" from "dead". Each wrong decision made the next server weaker.
A cluster needs to know which nodes are alive. It uses that list to route requests, place data and pick
leaders
But you saw in
Why distributed systems are hard
that silence has many causes. A node can be dead, paused, overloaded, or behind a bad link. The
SWIM
paper puts it plainly: a
process
that loses messages looks the same as one that has failed.
So a
failure detector
can only guess. Every design picks a point between two mistakes:
Too fast:
you mark healthy nodes dead. This is a false positive.
Too slow:
a dead node keeps getting traffic for a long time.
The key idea.
A failure detector does not find dead nodes. It finds nodes that are late. Choose how late counts as dead, and design what happens next so that a wrong guess is cheap.
Heartbeats and a fixed timeout
The simplest design: each node sends a
heartbeat
every second. If you hear nothing for, say, 5 seconds, you call the node dead.
Raft
uses this idea for leaders. A
follower
that hears no heartbeat for one
election timeout
starts an election. You can read more in
Consensus and Raft
A
load balancer
health check is the same idea, but it asks instead of waiting.
Load balancing
covers those settings.
A fixed
timeout
has a problem. A good value on a quiet network is too short on a busy one. The phi paper calls this the trade-off between conservative and aggressive detection.
Phi accrual: a score, not a yes or no
Hayashibara and others proposed the
phi accrual failure detector
in 2004. It does not answer "trust" or "suspect". It gives a suspicion level on a continuous scale. The level keeps rising while no heartbeat arrives.
The phi detector keeps a window of recent gaps between heartbeats. From these, it learns what "normal" looks like. Then it asks: how unlikely is it that the next heartbeat is still on its way?

blocks.v:
import math, statistics

def phi(now, last_beat, gaps):
    mean = statistics.mean(gaps)
    std = max(statistics.stdev(gaps), 0.1)  # avoid a zero spread
    late = now - last_beat
    # chance a heartbeat still arrives after this long
    p_later = 0.5 * math.erfc((late - mean) / (std * math.sqrt(2)))
    return -math.log10(max(p_later, 1e-300))

c.v: This is the formula Akka documents, using a normal curve.
Each step of 1 in phi means about ten times fewer mistakes. With a threshold of 1, about 10% of suspicions turn out wrong. With 2 it is about 1%, and with 3 about 0.1%.

Say heartbeats come every 1 second. With a spread of 0.1 seconds (the smallest the code allows), 1.6 seconds of silence gives phi of about 9. With a spread of 0.3 seconds, the same silence gives phi of only about 1.6. With a threshold of 8, the first node is suspected and the second is not. The detector adapts to the network you really have.
Akka and Cassandra both use a default threshold of 8.
Akka suggests 12 on cloud networks such as Amazon EC2.
A low threshold gives many wrong suspicions but finds crashes fast. A high one makes fewer mistakes but is slower.
SWIM: membership by gossip
Heartbeats raise a second problem: who talks to whom? If every node sends heartbeats to every other node, the network load grows with the square of the group size.
SWIM splits the job into two parts: failure detection and spreading the news.
Step through one probe round.

In each protocol period, a node pings one random member. If no ack comes in time, it sends a ping-req to k other members. They ping the target and relay any ack. This avoids blaming a node for congestion on one path.
If nobody gets an ack, the target is marked "suspect", not dead. A suspected node can refute this by sending an Alive message with a higher
incarnation number
. If the suspicion times out first, a Confirm message removes the node.
The news does not need its own messages. It rides on the pings and acks that are already flowing. The paper calls this infection-style dissemination.
The expected detection time and the load on each member do not grow with the size of the group.
SWIM is a
gossip protocol
: news spreads from node to node, with no central server.
Lifeguard: when the accuser is the slow one
The SWIM paper itself notes a weak spot. A slow process, for example one that drops
packets
from full buffers, can declare several healthy processes faulty.
HashiCorp hit this in memberlist, the library inside Serf, Consul and Nomad. CPU exhaustion, network delay or loss made members wrongly declare others faulty.
Their fix, Lifeguard, assumes the local failure detector may be the problem.
It has three parts:
Self-awareness.
A node keeps a score of signs that it is unhealthy itself. While the score is high, it is slower to accuse others.
Dogpile.
The suspicion timeout starts long and gets shorter as more members confirm the suspicion. A lone, slow accuser gets no support, so the target has time to refute.
Buddy system.
A suspected node is told directly in the probe it receives, so it can refute at once.
HashiCorp reports more than 50 times fewer false positives under CPU exhaustion. With the new memberlist defaults, failures were found 20% faster with 20 times fewer false positives.
After detection
Detection is only half of the story. The action you take next often does more damage.
Rebalancing
Data and traffic move off the "dead" node. HashiCorp notes that false accusations move traffic away from healthy members and cause needless data rebalancing.
Flapping
The node comes back, then is removed again. GitHub's role moved away and then back on one day.
Cascading failure
Moving work to the rest of the cluster adds load. In 2011, AWS EBS nodes that lost contact assumed their peers had failed.
They all searched for space for new copies at once. This "re-mirroring storm" left about 13% of volumes in one zone stuck.
Removing a slow node is not free. The work it held lands on the nodes that are left.
Fixed timeout, short
Pauses and slow links trip it.
Cheap actions, such as skipping a server for a few seconds.
Fixed timeout, long
Expensive actions, such as moving data.
Phi accrual
, on a steady network.
It adapts to jitter.
Peer-to-peer databases and actor systems such as Cassandra and Akka.
SWIM gossip with Lifeguard
Time does not grow with cluster size.
Indirect probes and suspicion help.
Large clusters that need a shared member list, such as Consul.
A human decides
Rare, risky moves, such as failing over a primary database.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Ask:
"What does this cluster do when it marks a node dead, and what does a wrong guess cost?"
Size the timeout to the cost of the action.
Use different thresholds for different actions. The phi paper's example: stop sending new work at a low level, and remove the worker only at a high one.
Know your longest normal pause:
garbage collection
, a big
compaction
, a slow disk. Your timeout must be longer.
Rate-limit removals. If many nodes "die" at once, suspect the network or the detector first.
When you see false positives, find the cause before you raise the threshold. Akka lists long GC pauses, overload and tight CPU limits.
Plan the rebalance. Check that the remaining nodes can take the extra load.
Make removal and rejoin cheap and gradual, so flapping does not move all the data each time.
"Read our cluster config. List every failure detection setting: heartbeat interval, timeouts, phi threshold, suspicion multiplier. For each, explain what action it triggers."
"Our Cassandra nodes are marked down during GC pauses. Show me how to confirm this from the logs, and compare raising the phi threshold with fixing the pauses."
"Write a test that pauses one node for 10 seconds in our 5-node cluster. Show what moves, how long it takes, and what happens when the node returns."
The agent did not raise every timeout without saying what gets slower. Longer detection means a dead node gets traffic for longer.
The proposed timeout is longer than your real worst pauses, taken from
metrics
, not guesses.
Automatic actions after detection have a limit, such as "remove at most one node per 10 minutes".
Any code that counts members handles a node that is "suspect", not only "alive" or "dead".
Next: leader election and
leases
, which use failure detection to pick one leader. Related:
Consensus and Raft
Sharding and consistent hashing
, and
Circuit breakers and bulkheads
. See
the GitHub incident page

q.v: Your failure detector uses a 2-second timeout. A healthy node has a 3-second garbage collection pause. What happens?

options.v: Nothing. The detector knows the node is only paused.
The node is marked dead, even though it is healthy. This is a false positive.
The node is marked dead only if it also stops answering health checks.

why.v: From the outside, a pause looks the same as a crash. Any silence longer than the timeout is treated as a failure.

q.v: What does a phi accrual failure detector give you instead of "alive" or "dead"?

options.v: A suspicion level that grows the longer a heartbeat is late, compared with past heartbeat gaps.
The exact time when the node crashed.
The number of nodes that agree the node is dead.

why.v: Phi is a score on a scale. Each application picks its own threshold, for example 8 in Akka and Cassandra by default.

q.v: In SWIM, node A gets no ack from node B. What does A do next?

options.v: It marks B as dead at once and tells everyone.
It sends a heartbeat to every member of the group.
It asks a few other members to ping B for it.

why.v: The indirect ping-req goes over other network paths. It stops one congested link from getting a healthy node removed.

q.v: Lifeguard adds "local health" to SWIM. What problem does that solve?

options.v: A slow or overloaded node wrongly accuses healthy nodes of being dead.
Gossip messages are too large for one network packet.
New nodes cannot find the cluster when they start.

why.v: If a node is slow itself, its missed acks are probably its own fault. Lifeguard makes such a node wait longer before it accuses others.
